library: AI Employee Lab Tech SFX Library
voice_reference: dialogue mixed to about -14 LUFS integrated

categories.name: Whooshes & Swishes (transition movement)
categories.when_to_use: Cuts that carry weight (new section, B-roll insert, location change), digital zoom / punch-in and zoom-out, whip pans, zoom-through transitions, text cards and graphics sliding or flying in, phone mockups or cards entering frame. Not on every jump cut: most cuts should stay silent.
categories.typical_duration: Short swish 0.15-0.4 s; standard cut whoosh 0.3-0.6 s (sources cite under 0.3 s for scene transitions, ~0.6 s typical, 400-500 ms to fill a half-second move); slow sweeps 1-3 s. Trim the tail before the next spoken word.
categories.mix_notes: Start before the cut and land the peak (fastest/loudest point) on the first frame of the new shot or the fastest moment of the move; one guide says start 10-20 ms before the camera move and nudge frame by frame. A whoosh placed entirely after the cut feels late. Level about -18 to -12 dB relative to dialogue, or roughly -20 to -25 dBFS peak with dialogue peaking at -6 dBFS; if it is clearly audible over the voice it is 5-8 dB too hot. High-pass at 80-100 Hz; slight 1-3 kHz presence helps on phones. Pan with on-screen direction. Dip music 3-6 dB under it if the mix is crowded. Heavy whooshes for big or slow moves, light or whip for fast cuts; a bright plastic whoosh breaks a dark mood. Index must store the peak offset so the agent can back-time it.

categories.name: Risers & Build-ups
categories.when_to_use: Before a reveal (result, number, product, before/after, the answer), into the hook payoff in the first seconds, before a chart spike or big stat, into a section change, under a countdown, 'watch this' moments.
categories.typical_duration: ~0.5 s hook riser at the open; 1-2 s for most short-form reveals; 2-4 s for big reveals; 4-6 s only for long builds. Stock fixed lengths (1, 2, 4 s) so the agent can back-time without stretching.
categories.mix_notes: Back-time so the peak lands exactly on the reveal frame, then follow with an impact, a whoosh, or a hard cut to silence (riser into silence then smash cut gives strong contrast). Use a separate build-up plus hit when the hit frame must be exact; boom risers bake the hit in. Layering a low rumble riser with a cymbal riser gives depth plus a bright lift. Drop or duck music before the reveal; if speech continues over it, start well under the voice and let it climb. Once or twice per clip at most. Index: peak_ms, length, key if pitched.

categories.name: Impacts, Booms & Sub Drops
categories.when_to_use: Hook first frame, the key point or stat landing, title or logo reveal, end of a riser, punch-in on an emphasis word, beat drop, smash cut to black or to the result, end-card CTA.
categories.typical_duration: Tight hits 0.2-0.6 s; booms 0.5-1.5 s; sub drops 1-3 s tail; trailer hits and braams 2-4 s tail (fade the tail if voice continues).
categories.mix_notes: Transient exactly on the frame (tens of ms matter). Layer sub + mid punch + high transient so the hit survives phone speakers (inference: phone speakers reproduce little sub, so a bare sub drop can vanish; check on a phone). Brief music duck or a music cut under the hit. Ration to about one big hit per 10-15 s or nothing feels important. Keep true peak under -1 dBTP at master. Long tails must not mask the next word.

categories.name: Glitches & Digital Distortion
categories.when_to_use: Glitch and screen-tear transitions, AI / hacking / 'the system broke' topics, pattern interrupts, text distorting in or out, switching between screen recordings, 'error' or 'wrong way' beats, pixel / LCD text effects.
categories.typical_duration: 0.1-0.8 s for transitions; stutters 0.2-0.5 s; textures 1-3 s.
categories.mix_notes: Sync stutter peaks to the visual glitch frames; on transitions treat it like a whoosh (peak on the cut). In tech videos a glitch can replace the whoosh on cuts to keep one sonic world. Tame 2-5 kHz harshness and sit slightly below whooshes. Overuse reads cheap quickly; stock both soft-digital and aggressive variants.

categories.name: UI Clicks, Taps & Buttons
categories.when_to_use: Every real cursor click or tap in a screen recording, buttons pressed in app demos, toggles, menu selections, a checklist item ticking, highlighting a UI element, snappy sequences showing several items quickly.
categories.mix_notes: On the exact click frame. Files must be trimmed to the first transient so the agent can drop them on-frame. Felt more than heard: roughly -25 to -20 dBFS with voice at -6. High-pass ~120 Hz, tame 2-5 kHz. Rotate 4-8 round-robin variants on rapid repeats to avoid the machine-gun effect; mono is fine. Only on clicks that actually happen on screen.

categories.name: Notifications, Alerts & Confirmations
categories.when_to_use: A stat or achievement appears, 'it worked' moments, task or render complete, a new DM / email / sale notification on screen, checklist completion, an error beat, a soft ding on a highlighted caption keyword.
categories.typical_duration: 0.15-0.8 s; notifications and success chimes up to about 500 ms.
categories.mix_notes: On the frame the element appears. Bright tones cut through, so sit them lower than feels natural (about -22 to -18 dBFS). Keep one tonal family (same patch, varied pitch and envelope): confirm rises, error falls or detunes, notification is a 2-3 note motif. Tag musical key so the agent avoids clashes with music. Use original designs, not OS or app system sounds (recommendation: trademark/copyright risk and they read as stock).

categories.name: UI Motion, Swipes & Slides
categories.when_to_use: Phone mockups swiping, scrolling a feed or site, UI panels animating in, cards or screenshots sliding onto the stage, app windows opening, dashboards building, cards orbiting the speaker.
categories.mix_notes: Softer and airier than camera whooshes; peak on the element's fastest frame; pan with direction. Sit 3-6 dB under transition whooshes so UI motion never competes with real cuts. Stock micro, small and medium sizes so the agent can scale with element size.

categories.name: Data, HUD & AI Processing
categories.when_to_use: AI generating or an agent working through steps, progress bars and % counters, dashboards and data viz building, futuristic HUD overlays, 'the AI is analyzing' moments, code or terminal scrolling.
categories.mix_notes: Run as a low bed under voice (about -30 to -25 dBFS) with a loopable flag in the index; end on the completion frame with a confirm chime or soft hit. Avoid dense high chatter under important words.

categories.name: Typing & Keyboard
categories.when_to_use: A prompt being typed into ChatGPT / Claude, search-bar typing, code on screen, text type-on animations, texting on a phone mockup, slash commands typing themselves. Ali Abdaal's guide: typing or text sounds whenever text comes on screen.
categories.typical_duration: Single key 30-80 ms; bursts 0.5-3 s; loops 5-10 s.
categories.mix_notes: Match density to the character-reveal speed and land an enter key on submit. Quiet (about -25 dBFS); no continuous clatter under voice. One keyboard type per video. Several burst and loop lengths so loops are not audible.

categories.name: Pops, Blips & Text Appear
categories.when_to_use: Text box, sticker, emoji or icon appears; bullet points or list items stack in; a stat number appears; a caption keyword is highlighted; thumbnail tiles pop onto a wall.
categories.mix_notes: On the appearance frame. A very short whoosh in front of a pop makes a static graphic feel like it moved. Ascending pitched variants for sequential items. Not on every caption word; keep it for emphasis. Dry, no long reverb tails, quiet.

categories.name: Camera & Photo
categories.when_to_use: Screenshots and freeze-frames, snapshot cards pinned one per beat, photo reveals, before/after stills, white-flash transitions (a CapCut course pairs shutters with transitions), punch-ins faking a camera zoom (lens servo).
categories.mix_notes: Shutter transient on the flash or freeze frame, paired with a white flash; around -20 dBFS. Vary shutter models across a run of snapshots.

categories.name: Phone & Device
categories.when_to_use: Phone mockups and floating-iPhone shots, 'I got a DM' / 'my phone blew up' moments, unlock reveals, phone-in-hand B-roll.
categories.mix_notes: A table vibration reads instantly as a notification and is less cliche than a ding. Do not use real OEM system sounds (recommendation: legal risk).

categories.name: Money & Commerce
categories.when_to_use: Revenue numbers, pricing reveals, 'made $X', cost savings, sales notifications, ROI stats, money jokes.
categories.mix_notes: On the frame the number lands. Ka-ching is literal and a bit comedic; for premium tech content prefer a sleek payment chime or coin clink plus a soft hit. Ration heavily.

categories.name: Counters, Tickers & Timers
categories.when_to_use: Numbers counting up in KPI and stat cards, percentage counters rolling to 100%, countdowns ('3 steps'), time claims ('in 30 seconds'), render or progress bars.
categories.typical_duration: Single tick 20-60 ms; rolls 0.5-5 s, loopable.
categories.mix_notes: Match tick rate to how fast the digits change and slow it with the easing; finish on a hit, ding or pop when the final number lands. Low level; loopable flag in the index.

categories.name: Sci-Fi Energy, Holograms & Power
categories.when_to_use: An AI agent or robot appearing, a logo forming from particles, unlock or upgrade moments, futuristic UI worlds, before/after transformations.
categories.mix_notes: Keep subtle; big sci-fi sounds make a reel feel like a game trailer. Power-down pairs with endings. Often layered with a whoosh or riser.

categories.name: Shimmers, Sparkles & Light Sweeps
categories.when_to_use: Highlighter swipes and light sweeps across text or logos, clean or premium reveals, before/after transformations, glass UI cards appearing.
categories.mix_notes: High-frequency content cuts through easily, so keep it low. A shimmer leading into a pop or soft hit polishes a reveal.

categories.name: Stingers, Tonal Hits & Logo Stings
categories.when_to_use: Title cards and section headers, branded intros and outros, logo reveals, end-card CTA, a dramatic statement.
categories.mix_notes: Tonal, so tag key and BPM so the agent avoids clashing with the music bed; can stand in for an impact when there is no music. A house signature sting per brand builds recognition.

categories.name: Drones, Ambiences & Beds
categories.when_to_use: Under hooks when the music drops, tension in storytelling sections, dead air under screen recordings, a 'working late on AI' vibe.
categories.mix_notes: Very low: about -40 to -25 dBFS (one guide: ambient bed at 20-40% of dialogue level). Fade in and out over 0.5-1 s, low-pass behind foreground sounds, mono-check for phase.

categories.name: Reverses, Suck-backs & Downlifters
categories.when_to_use: Leading into a hard cut or hit, returning to the speaker after B-roll, 'wait, rewind' beats, ending a sequence (a falling tone reads as an ending), winding down after a big hit.
categories.mix_notes: Reverse swells end exactly on the cut frame (peak at the end, so peak_ms = length). Downlifters start on the hit and fall away. Do not stack with a riser into the same frame.

categories.name: Tactile Foley: Paper, Pen, Tape & Desk
categories.when_to_use: Paper-cut, scrapbook or ransom-note graphics, highlighter swipes on headlines, notes or cards pinned up, checkmarks drawn, 'rip up the old way', receipts, unboxing.
categories.mix_notes: Match marker-stroke length to the animation (stock stretchable loops); paper rips on the tear frame. Organic textures break up an all-synthetic palette and read as premium.

categories.name: Electric Zaps & Sparks
categories.when_to_use: Power or energy emphasis, electric text effects, 'shock' moments, glitchy energy accents.
categories.mix_notes: Harsh; keep short and low, use sparingly.

categories.name: Reactions, Crowd & Human
categories.when_to_use: Social proof, comedic beats, 'wait, what' reactions; heartbeat for tension builds.
categories.mix_notes: Rarely right for premium tech content; keep short and under the voice.

categories.name: Comedic & Meme Accents
categories.when_to_use: Humor, sarcasm, pattern interrupts. Hormozi-style editing is described as using 'cartoony sound design', but premium tech edits use these sparingly.
categories.mix_notes: Many viral meme sounds are rips of copyrighted media: include only original recreations. One per video at most in premium content.

categories.name: Retro 8-bit & Game
categories.when_to_use: Gamification ('level up your workflow'), achievement unlocks, playful lists.
categories.mix_notes: Niche; keep in one 'playful' tone family so it does not clash with the clean tech palette.
